procedural_history.originating_court: High Court of Kerala at Ernakulam
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated 28.04.2017 of the High Court of Kerala at Ernakulam, in W. P. (Crl.) No. 149 of 2017
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The High Court issued a Judgment and Order dated 28.04.2017 in W. P. (Crl.) No. 149 of 2017.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant assailed the High Court's order, leading to the present appeal before the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal.

issue.issue_text: The scope of the writ of habeas corpus in matters concerning the personal choice and liberty of an adult, and whether the High Court can scrutinize such choices beyond ascertaining the legality of the detention.

facts: A father filed a writ of habeas corpus in the High Court, alleging his adult daughter was in the illegal custody of her partner (appellant no. 1).
The father's argument was that the marriage was invalid because the couple had not reached the legal marriageable age when it was solemnized.
The High Court accepted the father's plea and ordered that the daughter be placed in his custody.
law: The primary purpose of a writ of habeas corpus is to ensure that no individual is deprived of their liberty without the sanction of law.
An adult who has attained the age of majority has a fundamental right to make their own choices, including who to live with, under Articles 19 and 21 of the Constitution.
Courts cannot assume the role of a guardian ('parens patriae') for an adult and cannot allow parental concern or societal morals to override an adult's constitutional right of choice.

The court's inquiry in a habeas corpus petition for an adult is limited to determining if the person is being illegally detained. Once it is established that the adult is acting on their own free will and their choice is not illegal, the court's inquiry must end.
application: The Supreme Court found that the High Court had acted erroneously by going beyond the limited scope of a habeas corpus writ.
The High Court's focus on the validity of the marriage was irrelevant. The central issue was whether the daughter, being an adult, was being held against her will.

The Court emphasized that as an adult, the daughter has the freedom to choose her own path and decide who she wants to live with, even if it is in a 'live-in relationship' outside of a formal marriage.
By entrusting the daughter's custody to her father, the High Court improperly curtailed her personal liberty and her fundamental right to choice, which it is constitutionally bound to protect.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that in a habeas corpus proceeding involving an adult, the High Court's role is strictly limited to determining if the detention is illegal. The court cannot scrutinize the personal choices of an adult, such as their choice of partner or the validity of their marriage. Once the court ascertains that the adult is acting out of their own free will, it must respect their choice and set them at liberty. The High Court's order was therefore set aside.

issue.issue_text: Whether the expression of personal choice by an adult is a fundamental right under Articles 19 and 21 of the Constitution, limiting the court's inquiry in a habeas corpus petition.

facts: A father filed a habeas corpus petition, claiming his adult daughter was in the illegal custody of her partner (appellant no. 1).
The father argued that their marriage was invalid.
The High Court sided with the father and entrusted the daughter's custody to him.
The case was appealed to the Supreme Court, where it was established that the daughter was an adult (major).
law: The expression of personal choice by an adult is a fundamental right guaranteed under Articles 19 and 21 of the Constitution.
When an individual reaches the age of majority, they are entitled to make their own choices, and courts cannot assume the role of a guardian ('parens patriae').

The purpose of a habeas corpus writ is to determine if a person is illegally detained. The court's role is to produce the person, ascertain their independent choice, and release them from any illegal restraint.
Once it is clear that an adult has made a choice that does not violate any valid law, the court's inquiry must end.
Constitutional freedoms, such as the right to choice, are superior to societal values or morals.
application: The Supreme Court determined that the central issue was not the validity of the marriage, but the daughter's right as an adult to choose her own life.
The Court found that the High Court erred by focusing on parental concern and the marriage's validity instead of upholding the daughter's fundamental right to choice.
Since the daughter was an adult and had expressed her desire to be with her partner, she was not in illegal custody.
The Court stated that even if they were not legally married, two consenting adults have the right to live together.
By granting custody to the father, the High Court had impermissibly curtailed the daughter's constitutional right to liberty and personal choice.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court accepted that an adult's personal choice is a fundamental right. It concluded that in a habeas corpus petition, the court's inquiry is limited to whether the adult is being illegally detained. Once it was established that the daughter, being a major, had made a voluntary choice to live with her partner, the court's role was to respect that choice. Consequently, the Supreme Court set aside the High Court's order and affirmed the daughter's freedom to decide with whom she wants to live.

cases.case_name: Shafin Jahan v. Asokan K.M. & Ors.
cases.principle: To emphasize the due importance that the Constitution accords to the right of choice of an adult person.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: Parental love or concern cannot be allowed to override the fundamental constitutional right of an adult to choose their own marriage partner, and the duty of a court is to uphold this right, not to abridge it without a valid authority of law.
obiter: Sans lawful sanction, the centripodal value of liberty should allow an individual to write his/her script.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: In a writ of habeas corpus concerning an adult, the court's inquiry is limited to ascertaining whether the individual is illegally detained. Once the adult expresses a clear and independent choice that does not violate any valid law, the court's role concludes. The court cannot assume the position of a 'super guardian' or 'parens patriae' to scrutinize the wisdom, reasons, or potential influences behind that choice, as the expression of personal choice is a fundamental right under Articles 19 and 21 of the Constitution that is integral to individual identity and liberty.
legal_tests_applied: In a habeas corpus petition, the court's role is to: 1) ensure the detenue is produced before it, 2) ascertain the person's independent choice, and 3) ensure the person is released from any illegal restraint. The inquiry must end once it is clear that the adult's choice does not transgress any valid legal framework.
policy_considerations: The duty of a Constitutional Court is to be the protector of fundamental rights, to uphold them, and not to abridge their sphere without valid legal authority.

The expression of choice is an acceptance of individual identity, and its curtailment in deference to societal will or morals destroys the individualistic entity of a person, as social values are not above constitutionally guaranteed freedom.
The centripodal value of liberty allows an individual to 'write his/her script,' and the court must respect this autonomy.
Courts cannot be moved by the 'sentiment of the mother or the egotism of the father' to override the expressed choice of an adult.
Once an adult clearly states their choice before the court, 'that alone matters and that is the heart of the reasoning for this Court, which keeps all controversies at bay.'
